fact_text: For a working status of residence the accepting employer (or another authorised agent) applies to a Regional Immigration Bureau in Japan for a Certificate of Eligibility (CoE) before the employee applies for a visa; the CoE confirms in advance that the person meets the landing conditions, so the visa and landing checks are streamlined.
evidence_quote: applies for a certificate of eligibility for a status of residence (except for “Temporary Visitor” and “Permanent Resident”) in Japan beforehand

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the employee just applies for a Japanese work visa at the embassy. Actually the Japanese employer/sponsor must first obtain a Certificate of Eligibility from Immigration inside Japan; the visa is issued abroad only afterwards. Action: have the Japanese entity file the CoE application early — it drives the whole timeline.

fact_text: Third-country nationals admitted for a mid/long-term working status are issued their residence card (zairyu card) on arrival at Narita, Haneda, Chubu, Kansai, New Chitose, Hiroshima or Fukuoka airport. If landing anywhere else, the card is mailed to the home address after the moving-in notification is filed.
evidence_quote: A residence card is issued at the airport.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the visa sticker in the passport is the residence permit. Actually the physical residence card is the status document, issued at the seven major airports on entry (or posted later if you land elsewhere), and must be carried at all times. Action: enter via a major airport to receive the card immediately.

fact_text: Within 14 days of settling into a residence a mid/long-term resident must report their address at the municipal (city/ward) office, presenting the residence card. This moving-in notification creates the resident record (juminhyo) later used for My Number, health insurance and pension.
evidence_quote: Please report the place of residence by presenting a residence card to the municipal office where you live in within 14 days of the day when you decide a new place of residence

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed address registration is optional admin. Actually failing to notify the municipal office within 14 days without a justifiable reason is a statutory ground for revoking the status of residence. Action: register at the ward office in the first days after arrival.

fact_text: A resident on an employment status (e.g. Engineer/Specialist in Humanities/International Services) must notify the Immigration Services Agency within 14 days when their contracting organisation changes — including when the employment contract ends or they move to a new employer.
evidence_quote: through internet within 14 days of the day when change was made to the name or location of the organization including employer

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you only deal with Immigration at visa renewal. Actually changing or leaving your employer must be reported to Immigration within 14 days even when your status of residence itself does not change. Action: file the notification of the contracting organisation after any employer change.

fact_text: Japan runs a points-based Highly Skilled Professional system scoring academic background, career and annual income; reaching 70 points or more admits the applicant as a Highly Skilled Professional with benefits such as a 5-year period of stay, activities spanning multiple statuses, and relaxed permanent-residence timelines.
evidence_quote: get 70 points or more in total, they are admitted as

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a senior hire just gets a standard Engineer/Specialist visa. Actually scoring 70+ on the HSP points table unlocks a 5-year stay and a fast track to permanent residence. Action: score the assignee early — a high earner often already qualifies.

fact_text: A resident who holds a valid residence card and passport and leaves Japan intending to return within 1 year can use 'special re-entry permission' and is exempted from applying for a re-entry permit; they simply mark the ED card on departure.
evidence_quote: permission procedure at Regional Immigration Services Office will be exempted as long as they have Residence Card and valid Passport.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed every trip abroad needs a re-entry permit or the visa is lost. Actually a return within 1 year needs no permit (special re-entry), but you must be back within that year or the status of residence lapses and cannot be extended from abroad. Action: for longer absences obtain a full re-entry permit (valid up to 5 years) before leaving.

fact_text: Residents aged 20–59 must be enrolled in Japan's public pension system; company employees are enrolled by their employer in Employees' Pension Insurance (Category II) with contributions deducted from salary.
evidence_quote: The Japanese National Pension system is a public pension system in which those aged 20 to 59 years who reside in Japan are to enroll.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a foreign assignee can skip the Japanese pension. Actually enrolment is compulsory for residents aged 20–59 and the employer must enrol employees in Employees' Pension Insurance. Action: check whether a social-security (totalization) agreement lets the assignee stay in the home scheme with a certificate of coverage.

fact_text: Enrolment in public medical insurance is mandatory for registered residents: company employees join Employees' Health Insurance, and every other registered resident under 75 who is not in Employees' Health Insurance must enrol in National Health Insurance.
evidence_quote: All registered residents who are under 75 and are not in Employees’ Health Insurance are obliged to get enrolled in National Health Insurance.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed private or corporate travel insurance is enough. Actually every registered resident must belong to a Japanese public health-insurance scheme (Employees' or National). Action: confirm the employer enrols the assignee and dependents in Employees' Health Insurance.

fact_text: Every registered resident, including foreign nationals, is assigned a 12-digit Individual Number (My Number). It is required for everyday setup such as opening a bank account, receiving a pension, and making or receiving overseas remittances.
evidence_quote: When you open a bank account

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed My Number is only for Japanese citizens or only for taxes. Actually foreign residents receive one through their municipal registration and need it to open a bank account. Action: collect the My Number notification after registering your address, before opening accounts.

fact_text: For income-tax purposes a foreign national living in Japan is a 'non-permanent resident' if they have had a domicile or residence in Japan for an aggregate of five years or less within the preceding ten years.
evidence_quote: an aggregate period of five years or less within the preceding ten years is classified as a non-permanent resident

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you are either fully tax-resident (taxed on worldwide income) or not. Actually Japan has a middle 'non-permanent resident' category for foreigners in their first years. Action: track the 5-year clock — it changes what foreign income becomes taxable.

fact_text: A non-permanent resident is taxed on income other than foreign-source income, plus any foreign-source income that is paid in Japan or remitted to Japan from abroad; foreign-source income kept abroad is generally outside the Japanese tax base while in this category.
evidence_quote: (a) income other than foreign source income, (b) foreign source income paid in Japan and (c) foreign source income paid abroad and remitted to Japan from abroad

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed Japanese tax residents pay Japanese tax on worldwide income from day one. Actually a non-permanent resident's foreign-source income is taxed only to the extent paid in or remitted to Japan. Action: manage remittances into Japan carefully during the non-permanent-resident years.

fact_text: A foreign licence can be converted to a Japanese licence (gaimen kirikae) at a prefectural Driver's License Center; the holder is exempted from the full test if they pass the knowledge and skills check, but must have resided in the issuing country for at least three months after that licence was issued.
evidence_quote: After being licensed in a country, you must have resided for at least an additional three months there.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a foreign or international licence covers you indefinitely. Actually a translated/international licence is valid for at most one year, and conversion requires at least three months' residence in the issuing country after you obtained that licence. Action: gather proof of that 3-month residence before applying.

fact_text: A family member on a 'Dependent' (Family Stay) status may not work for pay until they obtain 'permission to engage in an activity other than that permitted'; taking paid work without it is a statutory ground for deportation.
evidence_quote: receiving remuneration without permission to engage in an activity other than those permitted under the status of residence previously granted

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a spouse on a dependent visa can simply take a job. Actually they must first obtain 'permission to engage in an activity other than that permitted', and only limited part-time work is authorised. Action: apply for the activity permission (available at the airport on arrival or at an Immigration office) before the spouse starts any paid work.
